Can We Inherit More Than DNA? What Mahalaya Amavasya Says About the Patterns Families Pass Down

You promised yourself you would never become like your parents.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:22
Instaread

Then one day, during an argument, you hear yourself saying your father’s exact words.

The same words.

The same tone.

And for a moment, you wonder:

“Where did that come from?”

We know that families pass down physical characteristics. Genetic testing can reveal remarkable information about ancestry and inherited health risks.

But families can pass down other things too.

How we deal with money.

How we express anger.

How comfortable we are showing affection.

How we respond to fear, failure, conflict, and even silence.

This is one reason the conversation around generational trauma has become so powerful.

And it is also why Mahalaya Amavasya, an ancient Hindu tradition centered on remembering and honoring ancestors, can feel surprisingly relevant to modern life.

Mahalaya asks us to remember those who came before us.

But perhaps it can also encourage us to ask:

“What from my family deserves to move forward with me?”

Generational Trauma Does Not Always Look Dramatic

Not every repeating family pattern looks extraordinary or obviously harmful.

Sometimes it is simply a sentence:

Family
Shop Puja Supplies

“We don’t discuss family problems outside the house.”

Sometimes it is a behavior.

Nobody apologizes after an argument. Everyone simply starts speaking again two days later.

Sometimes it involves money.

Imagine your grandfather grew up with very little.

For him, saving money was not a lifestyle choice. It was survival.

He taught your father that spending money was dangerous.

Now you have a stable career, savings, and a comfortable life.

Yet buying something for yourself still creates an uncomfortable feeling of guilt.

The financial danger disappeared decades ago.

The fear did not.

This is where discussions about family psychology and generational trauma become particularly relevant.

Science does not establish that every psychological trauma is simply encoded into DNA and passed unchanged from one generation to another.

Family patterns can travel through generations in much more direct ways.

Children watch how adults handle:

  • Conflict
  • Money
  • Relationships
  • Fear
  • Failure
  • Affection
  • Stress

They may carry those lessons into adulthood without consciously realizing where they learned them.

Sometimes something feels inherited simply because we learned it so early that we cannot remember learning it.

Mahalaya Amavasya Asks Us to Look at the People Who Came Before Us

Mahalaya Amavasya, also known as Sarva Pitru Amavasya, marks the concluding period of Pitru Paksha, the Hindu observance dedicated to remembering and honoring departed ancestors.

Families traditionally offer prayers and perform ancestral rituals such as Tarpan and Shraddha.

But step away from the ritual for a moment.

Imagine sitting at a table with photographs of your parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents.

You probably know some of their stories.

Others may have disappeared completely.

Yet pieces of their lives may still be visible in yours.

Your grandmother’s recipe.

Your father’s work ethic.

Your mother’s habit of making sure everyone reached home safely.

Your grandfather’s fear of debt.

Your family’s discomfort with discussing emotions.

The silence that appears whenever conflict enters the room.

Suddenly, family history becomes more than names, photographs, and dates.

It becomes a much more personal question:

“What are we still carrying from the people who came before us?”

You Can Love Your Family Without Repeating Everything

This is where Mahalaya can take on a particularly meaningful dimension.

Honoring your ancestors does not require believing that they were perfect.

And choosing differently does not necessarily mean rejecting them.

Perhaps your grandmother remained silent because women of her generation had fewer choices.

You can respect her strength without inheriting her silence.

Perhaps your father rarely said, “I love you,” because his own father never said those words to him.

You can understand that history and still tell your own children you love them every day.

Perhaps your parents remained in an unhappy relationship because separation was financially or socially difficult.

Understanding their circumstances does not require adopting their decision as your own definition of love.

Sometimes emotional healing begins when we stop asking:

“Who should I blame?”

And begin asking:

“What would I like to do differently?”

That question gives the present generation somewhere to go.

Breaking Family Cycles Rarely Looks Dramatic

When people hear the phrase “breaking family cycles,” they may imagine a dramatic confrontation or a life-changing announcement.

Usually, it happens much more quietly.

It is the father who apologizes to his child because nobody ever apologized to him.

It is the daughter who finally says no without spending the next three days feeling guilty.

It is the couple who chooses counseling instead of pretending nothing is wrong.

It is the parent who tells a son that crying does not make him weak.

It is the family that finally talks about something everyone has avoided for twenty years.

No dramatic announcement.

No grand speech.

Just one person quietly deciding:

“This particular pattern does not need another generation.”

Try Asking Yourself This One Question on Mahalaya

You do not need a complicated psychological exercise to reflect on your family patterns.

Take a piece of paper and write two sentences:

“From my family, I want to carry forward…”

And:

“With me, I want to end…”

Your first list might include:

  • Resilience
  • Loyalty
  • Faith
  • Humor
  • Generosity
  • Ambition
  • Family meals
  • Cultural traditions
  • Care for one another

Your second might include:

  • Constant criticism
  • Financial anxiety
  • Emotional silence
  • Explosive arguments
  • Fear of asking for help
  • Unhealthy guilt
  • Avoiding difficult conversations

This exercise is not about diagnosing your family.

It is not an invitation to create a list of everything your parents did wrong.

It is simply an opportunity to notice.

And if that reflection reveals severe trauma, abuse, or continuing emotional distress, professional mental health support can offer something that a spiritual ritual or online article cannot.

Family Patterns Can Continue Without Anyone Intending Them To

One of the most interesting things about family patterns is that nobody necessarily decides to create them.

A parent may simply repeat what they experienced as a child.

Then their child grows up believing that behavior is normal.

The pattern continues.

This can happen with money.

With relationships.

With communication.

With parenting.

With anger.

Even with the way families express love.

Awareness does not automatically solve every problem.

But it can create something extremely important:

A choice.

Once you recognize a pattern, you can begin asking whether it still belongs in your life.

Emotional Healing Does Not Require Erasing the Past

Healing is sometimes misunderstood as forgetting.

But remembering and healing can exist together.

You can remember what happened without allowing it to control every decision you make today.

You can understand why someone behaved a certain way without deciding that their behavior was acceptable.

You can appreciate what your family gave you while acknowledging what was difficult.

And you can change a pattern without pretending your family history never existed.

That balance fits naturally with the deeper reflective spirit of Mahalaya Amavasya.

Remembering the past does not mean becoming trapped inside it.

Perhaps Inheritance Is About More Than What We Receive

At its heart, Mahalaya Amavasya centers on remembrance, gratitude, and honoring ancestors.

But remembrance can have a powerful side effect.

It creates awareness.

You begin to recognize that not every habit you carry began with you.

Some came from people you loved.

Some came from people who were simply trying to survive.

Some may have protected your family once but no longer serve the same purpose today.

And that leads to perhaps the most important question of all:

“What will I pass to the next generation?”

One Day, You May Be Someone’s Ancestor Too

You are not only someone’s child or grandchild.

One day, you may also become someone’s ancestor.

A child may remember how you responded when they were angry.

Someone’s relationship with money may be influenced by watching yours.

The way you express affection—or avoid expressing it—may travel further than you realize.

Your approach to failure may become somebody else’s internal voice.

Your willingness to apologize may teach another generation that saying “I was wrong” is a sign of strength rather than weakness.

That means inheritance is not only about asking:

“What did my family give me?”

It is also about asking:

“What am I preparing to give those who come after me?”

Final Thoughts

This Mahalaya Amavasya, remember those who came before you.

Carry forward their strength.

Preserve their stories.

Keep the love, laughter, traditions, recipes, resilience, and wisdom worth preserving.

But if fear, silence, anger, guilt, or pain has already traveled far enough through your family history, it does not automatically need another destination.

You can respect where you came from without repeating everything that came with it.

You can honor your ancestors while making different choices.

And perhaps that is one of the most powerful ways to think about inheritance.

You may inherit the story, but you still have a say in how the next chapter is written.
